opus-5.5.text:
I should say up front that I'm not close to Harvey's customer base, so I can't speak to what any particular firm told them. But I can tell you the pattern I see across law firms and other professional services businesses experimenting with generative AI, and I suspect it applies.

The most thoughtful early adopters aren't just asking, "How do I make my associates 20% faster at drafting a memo?" That's useful, but it's the incremental view. The more revealing question they're starting to ask is, "If the cost of a certain kind of cognitive work drops by 10x or more, what does my business look like?"

That's uncomfortable for a lot of professional services firms, because many are built on the billable hour. If AI lets you do in one hour what used to take ten, a pure hourly model means you've just cut your revenue. So the forward-looking firms are rethinking pricing. They're moving toward fixed fees or value-based pricing, and asking which services they could offer that weren't economical before.

That last part is what excites me. When something gets much cheaper, you often get a lot more of it. There's a huge amount of unmet demand for legal help: small businesses that can't afford a contract review, individuals who never see a lawyer at all. If AI lowers the cost enough, firms that figure out how to serve those markets could grow, not shrink.

The other thing I find telling is workflow. The firms getting real value aren't just handing lawyers a chatbot. They're breaking their work into tasks, figuring out which ones AI can do or assist with, and redesigning the process around that. That's the same playbook I'd recommend to any business. Don't think about automating jobs. Think about automating tasks, then reimagine the workflow.

So the early adopters see that this isn't a productivity tool bolted onto the old business. It's a chance, and frankly a pressure, to rethink what the business is.

r001.rationale: The response describes early adopters planning for AI to make cognitive work much cheaper and using that prospect to rethink pricing, services, and workflows.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss reduced associate hiring or how that could shrink the future pool of partner candidates.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find revealing is that the firms leaning in hardest aren't the ones trying to use AI to do the same work with fewer people. They're the ones asking a different question, which is: what does a law firm even look like when the cost of a first draft, or a first pass at document review, drops by an order of magnitude?

Legal has an interesting economic structure because so much of it has been priced by the hour. If a tool lets an associate do in twenty minutes what used to take six hours, the naive view is that you've just lost five hours of billing. The early adopters I talk to understand that this is the wrong frame. What they're actually seeing is that the bottleneck shifts. The scarce thing is no longer producing the work product; it's judgment, client relationships, and being able to take on matters you previously couldn't afford to staff. So they're starting to think about fixed-fee work, about going after smaller clients that were never economical before, and about what their training pipeline for junior lawyers looks like when the junior lawyers aren't spending their first two years on document review.

The other thing I notice is a pattern I've seen in every wave of technology adoption. The firms that do well aren't necessarily the most technical. They're the ones where a partner, someone with real authority, actually sits down and uses the tool on real matters, builds intuition for where it's good and where it falls apart, and then redesigns the workflow around that. The ones that struggle tend to treat it as an IT procurement decision, buy seats, and then wonder why nothing changed. That gap between buying AI and actually integrating it into how work gets done is where most of the value is, and it's also where most of the failures are.

And I'd say the honest early adopters are also quite clear-eyed about the limits. They know the model hallucinates citations sometimes, they build review steps around that, and they don't pretend otherwise. That kind of sober, hands-on realism combined with real ambition about the business model is, I think, exactly the posture that ends up winning.

r001.rationale: The response says early adopters are rethinking what a law firm looks like as AI makes core work much cheaper, and describes business model and workflow changes they are considering.

r002.rationale: It mentions how AI may change junior lawyers’ training, but does not say reduced associate hiring could shrink the future pool of partners.

astra-6.text:
What I find revealing is whether they see AI as a way to do the same work with fewer people, or as a way to do much more work. For a law firm, if your starting point is, “We bill by the hour, and now this takes fewer hours,” that can feel threatening. But if your starting point is, “There’s a lot of legal work that clients need but can’t currently afford,” then making lawyers more productive creates an opportunity to serve that demand.

So the interesting question is whether the business model can evolve along with the technology. Can you charge for the value you deliver rather than the time it takes? The early adopters thinking that way are asking a much bigger question than which tasks they can automate. They’re asking what their firm could become.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI-enabled productivity and evolving law firm business models, but it does not identify planning for a future where AI is ubiquitous.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reduced associate hiring or the resulting smaller pool of future partners.

sol-6.1.text: What I find revealing is that some of the early adopters are asking, “How do we use AI to grow our business?” If you can do legal work more efficiently, you can serve clients or take on matters that previously wouldn’t have made economic sense. So the opportunity goes beyond doing the same work at lower cost. It opens up the question of what your business could become when you can deliver much more legal work with the team you have.

r001.rationale: The response describes using AI to grow a business and serve more clients, but does not identify a future of ubiquitous AI as the revealing shift.
